title: The good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37)
hook: a priest and a Levite pass by, and the despised foreigner stops
tomorrow: the lost sheep and the lost coin

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mustard seed and the leaven, the yeast hidden in the dough. Your line was small is how it starts. What tiny good thing did you plant? Day forty-five.

A scholar of the Law stands up to test Jesus. What must I do to have eternal life? Jesus turns it back: what does the Law say? And the man answers well: love God with all your heart, soul, strength and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. Right, says Jesus. Do this, and you'll live. But the man wants to pin it down. He wants to know where the edges are. In the Douay-Rheims: "And who is my neighbour?" Who counts, and who doesn't? It's a question about where love is allowed to stop. And Jesus doesn't give him a definition. He tells him a story. Today: the story he tells instead.
screen: `WHAT MUST I DO?` → `LOVE GOD, LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.` → `AND WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR?`

segments.voice: A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The road goes down through lonely country, and on it he falls among robbers. He's stripped, beaten and left half dead. A priest comes down the road, sees him, and passes by on the other side. A Levite, who served in the Temple, does the same. The story never says why. People have guessed for centuries, but Jesus doesn't tell us, and he doesn't need to. Then a Samaritan comes. To the people listening, a Samaritan was a neighbor from across a long and bitter religious divide. And this one, Luke says, is moved with compassion. The Greek word comes from the gut, a feeling in your insides. He goes to the man, pours oil and wine on his wounds, bandages them, puts him on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays for his care. Two pence, the Douay-Rheims says, and a promise to cover anything more. Then Jesus asks the scholar: "Which of these three, in thy opinion, was neighbour to him that fell among the robbers?" Notice what happened. The man asked, who is my neighbor, who do I have to love? Jesus answers a different question: who acted like a neighbor? The scholar doesn't say the word Samaritan. He says: the one who showed him mercy. And Jesus says: "Go, and do thou in like manner." Early Church writers also read the story another way: Christ as the Samaritan, the wounded man as all of us, the inn as the Church. Pope Francis gave a whole chapter of his letter Fratelli Tutti to this road.
screen: `THE ROAD DOWN TO JERICHO.` · `TWO PASS BY. ONE STOPS.` · `MOVED IN HIS GUT.` · `NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO PROVED NEIGHBOR.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for someone today. Settle and breathe. Think about the roads you'll walk today, the hallways, the streets, the feeds. Who's lying by the side of them? Not always bleeding. Sometimes just lonely, or overwhelmed, or ignored. Picture one person you usually pass by on the other side. Now picture stopping. What would it cost you? Ten minutes? A little awkwardness? If you pray, you can ask for the Samaritan's gut-deep compassion. The bell holds the time.
Samaritan. A stranger from across a bitter divide, the one who stopped and showed mercy on the Jericho road.
Your line: who proved neighbor. Today, don't ask who deserves your help. Stop for one person, and be the neighbor. Day forty-five.

screen: `DAY 45 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LOST SHEEP AND THE LOST COIN.`

howItsDone: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass and in teaching on the works of mercy; Pope Francis's encyclical Fratelli Tutti gives a chapter to it, and some Catholic hospitals and charities take the Samaritan as their model.

fork.setup: you're a scholar of the Law. you ask Jesus, who is my neighbor? what does he do?
options: give you a clear list of who counts.
tell you a story and ask who acted like a neighbor.
tell you everyone is your neighbor and move on.
fork.reveal: he tells the story of the man on the Jericho road, then asks who proved neighbor. and he ends: “Go, and do thou in like manner.”

original.note: Greek: he was moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inward parts, the gut.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice story about helping strangers.
what it means: a question about who counts, answered with a story that asks who acted like a neighbor, and the hero is the outsider.
what a scholar hears: esplanchnisthē, a compassion felt in the gut. early Church writers also read the Samaritan as Christ, and the inn as the Church.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 10:29, 10:36 and 10:37 given from memory; confirm.
The Jerusalem–Jericho road descends roughly 3,000+ feet over about 17–18 miles; the script says 'thousands of feet'. Confirm.
The priest and Levite are presented without speculation about purity rules, to avoid framing Jewish law negatively. Confirm this is careful.
'Two days' wages' for the two denarii (10:35): standard estimate; confirm.
Allegorical reading (Christ as Samaritan, inn as Church) is found in Origen and Augustine; confirm attribution to 'early Church writers'.
Fratelli Tutti chapter 2, 'A stranger on the road', is a reflection on this parable; confirm.

Editor review 2026-10-01: Fratelli Tutti corrected: it gives one chapter to the parable, not the whole letter; cut "thousands of feet", "two days' wages" (now the Douay-Rheims "two pence"), "the most famous answer" and "a question we all ask"; no longer reads the scholar's mind.
